presEras.label: Santa Anna to the Restored Republic
presEras.blurb: Mexico's mid-century elections were indirect, held between coups and wars: Santa Anna's last dictatorship, the Reforma and Benito Juárez's embattled presidencies through French intervention, and the disputed 1876 contest that ended in Porfirio Díaz's revolt.

presEras.label: The Porfiriato
presEras.blurb: Porfirio Díaz was re-elected seven times in contests with no real opposition, the machinery of a personal dictatorship dressed as a republic. The fraudulent 1910 election against the jailed Francisco Madero lit the Mexican Revolution.

presEras.label: Revolution and reconstruction
presEras.blurb: Madero's 1911 landslide was Mexico's freest election yet — followed by his murder, civil war, the 1917 Constitution, and the assassination-scarred rise of the Sonoran generals. The 1929 special election, won by the brand-new official party amid open fraud, founded the system that would rule for seven decades.

presEras.label: The PRI's hegemony
presEras.blurb: For sixty years the official party — PNR, then PRM, then PRI — never lost a presidential election, blending real social bases with electoral control. The arc runs from Cárdenas's oil nationalism to the 1988 'fall of the system', when the count mysteriously crashed with the opposition ahead.

presEras.label: Transition and alternation
presEras.blurb: Reformed electoral institutions turned real: Fox's 2000 victory ended 71 years of one-party rule, 2006 was decided by half a point, the PRI returned in 2012, and Morena's landslides in 2018 and 2024 — the latter electing Claudia Sheinbaum, Mexico's first woman president — built a new dominant party.

legEras.label: Midterms under the hegemonic party
legEras.blurb: Chamber of Deputies midterms under PRI rule were rituals of an official majority, though reforms from 1963 onward carved out token, then real, opposition seats — the laboratory where Mexico's opposition slowly learned to win.

legEras.label: The plural Chamber
legEras.blurb: In 1997 the PRI lost its Chamber majority for the first time, and every midterm since has been a genuine referendum on the sitting president — from Fox's divided government through the PRI's 2009 comeback to Morena's defence of its supermajority in 2021.

presidential.summary: Presidential elections were held in Mexico in April 1853, following the resignation of Mariano Arista on January 5. The country experienced profound political polarization between liberal and conservative factions, alongside economic and military instability as a result of the Mexican-American War.
presidential.caveat: An indirect election held amid deep instability; the franchise and the count were controlled by the government of the day.

presidential.summary: General elections were held in Mexico in September 1857. They were the first to be held under the February 1857 constitution, which introduced direct elections for the presidency, abolished the Senate, and introduced universal male suffrage for citizens aged 18 (if married) or 20 (if single), as long as they had an "honest mode of living".
presidential.caveat: An indirect election held amid deep instability; the franchise and the count were controlled by the government of the day.

presidential.summary: General elections were held in Mexico in 1861. Although incumbent president Benito Juárez received a majority (53%) of the popular vote, opponents claimed his margin of victory was not enough and a Congressional vote was required.
presidential.caveat: An indirect election held amid deep instability; the franchise and the count were controlled by the government of the day.

presidential.summary: General elections were held in Mexico on 11 July 1904. Incumbent Porfirio Díaz was the only serious candidate for the presidency, and was re-elected with 100% of the vote.
presidential.caveat: An election in form only: under the Porfiriato the result was arranged in advance and no genuine opposition was permitted. Recorded here as history, not as a free election.

presidential.summary: Porfirio Díaz, a liberal general who had distinguished himself during the War of Reform and resistance to French intervention, seized control of the Mexican government from Sebastian Lerdo de Tejada in an 1876 coup d'état, in which Díaz and other Mexican military officials explicitly opposed presidential re-election.
presidential.caveat: An election in form only: under the Porfiriato the result was arranged in advance and no genuine opposition was permitted. Recorded here as history, not as a free election.

presidential.summary: The 1910 elections were intended to be the first free elections of the Porfiriato, but after opposition leader Francisco I. Madero appeared poised to upset the Porfirian regime, he was arrested and imprisoned before the election was held.

General elections were held in Mexico on 1 July 1928. Alvaro Obregón was the only candidate in the presidential elections, and was elected unopposed.

The National Revolutionary Party, founded in 1928 by Mexico's most powerful leader at the time, Plutarco Elías Calles, made its debut in these elections. The 1929 elections marked the beginning of 71 uninterrupted years of rule by that party, which was later renamed Party of the Mexican Revolution in 1938 and finally, Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) in 1946.
presidential.caveat: Held under the hegemonic-party system: opposition parties appeared on the ballot, but the machinery of state made the official candidate's victory a foregone conclusion.

presidential.summary: The 1934 campaign and elections took place during the final phase of the period known as the Maximato; since 1924, Plutarco Elías Calles (self-proclaimed “Maximum Leader of the Revolution”) had been the most powerful figure in the country (between 1924 and 1928 de jure, as President, and from 1928 onward de facto as the “power behind the throne” while three presidents succeeded
presidential.caveat: Held under the hegemonic-party system: opposition parties appeared on the ballot, but the machinery of state made the official candidate's victory a foregone conclusion.

presidential.summary: General elections were held in Mexico on 7 July 1940. The presidential elections were won by Manuel Ávila Camacho, who received 94% of the vote.
presidential.caveat: Held under the hegemonic-party system: opposition parties appeared on the ballot, but the machinery of state made the official candidate's victory a foregone conclusion.

presidential.summary: With the establishment of the Federal Electoral Law of 1946, three political parties were registered: the National Action Party (PAN), the Mexican Democratic Party (PDM) and the Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI), with the latter being a successor of the Party of the Mexican Revolution.
presidential.caveat: Held under the hegemonic-party system: opposition parties appeared on the ballot, but the machinery of state made the official candidate's victory a foregone conclusion.

presidential.summary: General elections were held in Mexico on 7 July 1952. The presidential elections were won by Adolfo Ruiz Cortines of the Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI), who received 74.3% of the vote.
presidential.caveat: Held under the hegemonic-party system: opposition parties appeared on the ballot, but the machinery of state made the official candidate's victory a foregone conclusion.

presidential.summary: General elections were held in Mexico on 6 July 1958. The presidential elections were won by Adolfo López Mateos, who received 90.4% of the vote.
presidential.caveat: Held under the hegemonic-party system: opposition parties appeared on the ballot, but the machinery of state made the official candidate's victory a foregone conclusion.

presidential.summary: The 1964 election was the first to use the party deputy mechanism: a form of proportional representation through which three parties other than the hegemonic Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) – none of which won any first-past-the-post districts – were allocated 32 seats.
presidential.caveat: Held under the hegemonic-party system: opposition parties appeared on the ballot, but the machinery of state made the official candidate's victory a foregone conclusion.

presidential.summary: General elections were held in Mexico on 5 July 1970. The presidential elections were won by Luis Echeverría, who received 86% of the vote.
presidential.caveat: Held under the hegemonic-party system: opposition parties appeared on the ballot, but the machinery of state made the official candidate's victory a foregone conclusion.

presidential.summary: General elections were held in Mexico on 4 July 1976. José López Portillo was the only candidate in the presidential election, and was elected unopposed.
presidential.caveat: Held under the hegemonic-party system: opposition parties appeared on the ballot, but the machinery of state made the official candidate's victory a foregone conclusion.

presidential.summary: General elections were held in Mexico on 4 July 1982. The presidential elections were won by Miguel de la Madrid, who received 74% of the vote.
presidential.caveat: Held under the hegemonic-party system: opposition parties appeared on the ballot, but the machinery of state made the official candidate's victory a foregone conclusion.

presidential.summary: General elections were held in Mexico on 6 July 1988. They were the first competitive presidential elections in Mexico since the Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) took power in 1929.
presidential.caveat: Held under the hegemonic-party system; the vote count was interrupted and the official result is widely regarded as fraudulent.

presidential.summary: General elections were held in Mexico on 21 August 1994. The presidential elections resulted in a victory for Ernesto Zedillo of the Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI), whilst the PRI won 300 of the 500 seats in the Chamber of Deputies and 95 of the 128 seats in the Senate.

General elections were held in Mexico on Sunday, 2 July 2000. Voters went to the polls to elect a new president to serve a single six-year term, replacing President Ernesto Zedillo Ponce de León, who was ineligible for re-election under the 1917 Constitution.
General elections were held in Mexico on Sunday, 2 July 2006.

Several local ballots were held on the same day, including the election of a new Head of Government and new Legislative Assembly of the Federal District, gubernatorial elections in six states (Chiapas, Guanajuato, Jalisco, Morelos, Tabasco and Yucatán) and municipal and local congressional elections several states.

General elections were held in Mexico on 1 July 2018. Voters elected a new president to serve a six-year term, 128 members of the Senate for six years and 500 members of the Chamber of Deputies for three years.

General elections were held in Mexico on 2 June 2024. Voters elected a new president to serve a six-year term, all 500 members of the Chamber of Deputies, and all 128 members of the Senate of the Republic.

legislative.summary: Legislative elections were held in Mexico on 3 July 1949. The Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI), a dominant party that ruled the nation under an authoritarian regime, won 142 of the 147 seats in the Chamber of Deputies.

legislative.summary: Legislative elections were held in Mexico on 4 July 1955. They were first federal elections in which women were able to vote after President Adolfo Ruiz Cortines introduced unrestricted citizenship for women on 17 October 1953, meeting one of his main campaign promises.

legislative.summary: Legislative elections were held in Mexico on 18 August 1991, alongside gubernatorial elections in six states. The Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) won 320 of the 500 seats in the Chamber of Deputies and 31 of the 32 seats up for election in the Senate.

Legislative elections were held in Mexico on 6 July 1997. The Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) won 239 of the 500 seats in the Chamber of Deputies, the first time it had failed to win a majority.

According to polls, many voters were disappointed in President Vicente Fox for not fulfilling his campaign promises to create millions of jobs upon his election in July 2000, even though his approval ratings remained high.

A none of the above movement, dubbed "voto en blanco", or "blank vote", had arisen in response to the perceived corruption of the three major parties running in this election. Starting as a small group on blogs and YouTube, the movement had expanded its ranks, with politicians and intellectuals, such as Jose Antonio Crespo, supporting the movement.

The 500 members of the Chamber of Deputies were elected by two methods; 300 were elected in single-member constituencies and 200 by proportional representation in a single nationwide constituency. Constitutional reforms in 2014 led to the creation of the National Electoral Institute, replacing the Federal Electoral Institute.

Legislative elections were held in Mexico on 6 June 2021. Voters elected 500 deputies (300 in single-member constituencies by first-past-the-post and 200 by proportional representation) to sit in the Chamber of Deputies for the 65th Congress.
